claim: Seasonal coronaviruses (OC43, 229E, NL63, and HKU1) are endemic to the human population.
source: Seasonal coronaviruses (OC43, 229E, NL63, and HKU1) are endemic to the human population, regularly infecting and reinfecting humans while typically causing asymptomatic to mild respiratory infections.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about seasonal coronaviruses.

claim: Seasonal coronaviruses regularly infect and reinfect humans.
source: Seasonal coronaviruses (OC43, 229E, NL63, and HKU1) are endemic to the human population, regularly infecting and reinfecting humans while typically causing asymptomatic to mild respiratory infections.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the behavior of seasonal coronaviruses.

claim: Seasonal coronaviruses typically cause asymptomatic to mild respiratory infections.
source: Seasonal coronaviruses (OC43, 229E, NL63, and HKU1) are endemic to the human population, regularly infecting and reinfecting humans while typically causing asymptomatic to mild respiratory infections.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about disease severity.

claim: OC43 and 229E are undergoing adaptive evolution in regions of the viral spike protein exposed to human humoral immunity.
source: We provide evidence that at least two of these viruses, OC43 and 229E, are undergoing adaptive evolution in regions of the viral spike protein that are exposed to human humoral immunity.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple computational analyses presented in the results section.

claim: Reinfection by seasonal coronaviruses may be due in part to positively selected genetic changes that enable immune escape.
source: This suggests that reinfection may be due, in part, to positively selected genetic changes in these viruses that enable them to escape recognition by the immune system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the evidence of adaptive evolution in the spike protein.

claim: Adaptive changes in antigenic regions of seasonal coronaviruses may necessitate continual vaccine reformulation.
source: It is possible that, as with seasonal influenza, these adaptive changes in antigenic regions of the virus would necessitate continual reformulation of a vaccine made against them.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about vaccine implications based on the findings.

claim: OC43 and 229E were identified as causative agents of roughly 15% of common colds.
source: At this time, two species of HCoV, OC43 and 229E, were identified as the causative agents of roughly 15% of common colds (McIntosh, 1974; Heikkinen and Järvinen, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Infections with seasonal coronaviruses exhibit seasonal patterns, peaking in January to March in the Northern Hemisphere.
source: Infections with these viruses were shown to exhibit seasonal patterns, peaking in January to March in the Northern Hemisphere, as well as yearly variation, with the greatest incidence occurring every 2–4 years (Monto and Lim, 1974; Hamre and Beem, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Seasonal coronavirus infections show yearly variation with greatest incidence occurring every 2-4 years.
source: Infections with these viruses were shown to exhibit seasonal patterns, peaking in January to March in the Northern Hemisphere, as well as yearly variation, with the greatest incidence occurring every 2–4 years (Monto and Lim, 1974; Hamre and Beem, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Four HCoVs are endemic to the human population: OC43, 229E, HKU1, and NL63.
source: Subsequently, two additional seasonal HCoVs, HKU1 and NL63, have entered the human population. These four HCoVs endemic to the human population usually cause mild respiratory infections, but occasionally result in more severe disease in immunocompromised patients or the elderly (Liu et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Endemic HCoVs occasionally result in more severe disease in immunocompromised patients or the elderly.
source: These four HCoVs endemic to the human population usually cause mild respiratory infections, but occasionally result in more severe disease in immunocompromised patients or the elderly (Liu et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Three additional HCoVs (SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2) have emerged in the past 20 years.
source: In the past 20 years, three additional HCoVs (SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2) have emerged, which cause more severe respiratory illness.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about recent coronavirus emergence.

claim: SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2 cause more severe respiratory illness than endemic HCoVs.
source: In the past 20 years, three additional HCoVs (SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2) have emerged, which cause more severe respiratory illness.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about disease severity.

claim: No vaccine for any HCoV was available at the time of writing.
source: At the writing of this paper, amidst the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, no vaccine for any HCoV is currently available, though many candidate SARS-CoV-2 vaccines are in production and clinical trials (Krammer, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the state of vaccine development at the time of writing, with citation support.

claim: Many candidate SARS-CoV-2 vaccines were in production and clinical trials at the time of writing.
source: At the writing of this paper, amidst the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, no vaccine for any HCoV is currently available, though many candidate SARS-CoV-2 vaccines are in production and clinical trials (Krammer, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citation support.

claim: Coronaviruses have a positive-sense RNA genome of roughly 30 kB.
source: Inside these virions is a positive-sense RNA genome of roughly 30 kB (Li, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Large genome size can accommodate more genetic variation than a smaller genome.
source: This large genome size can accommodate more genetic variation than a smaller genome (Woo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: RNA virus polymerases are error-prone.
source: Genome flexibility, coupled with a RNA virus error-prone polymerase (Drake, 1993) and a high rate of homologous recombination (Pasternak et al., 2006), creates genetic diversity that is acted upon by evolutionary pressures that select for viral replication.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Coronaviruses have a high rate of homologous recombination.
source: Genome flexibility, coupled with a RNA virus error-prone polymerase (Drake, 1993) and a high rate of homologous recombination (Pasternak et al., 2006), creates genetic diversity that is acted upon by evolutionary pressures that select for viral replication.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Genetic diversity in coronaviruses contributes to their ability to jump species barriers.
source: This spawns much of the diversity within and between coronaviruses species (Woo et al., 2009; Hon et al., 2008) and can contribute to the virus' ability to jump species-barriers, allowing a previously zoonotic CoV to infect and replicate in humans.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Antigenic evolution leaves a characteristic mark of positively selected epitopes within viral proteins most exposed to the host immune system.
source: Antigenic evolution, or antigenic drift, leaves a characteristic mark of positively selected epitopes within the viral proteins most exposed to the host immune system (Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The spike protein is the coronavirus protein most exposed to human humoral immunity.
source: For CoVs, this is the spike protein, exposed on the surface of the virion to human humoral immunity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about coronavirus biology.

claim: Seasonal influenza evolves antigenically.
source: Some human respiratory illnesses caused by RNA viruses, like seasonal influenza (Smith et al., 2004), evolve antigenically, while others, like measles, do not (Fulton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Measles does not evolve antigenically.
source: Some human respiratory illnesses caused by RNA viruses, like seasonal influenza (Smith et al., 2004), evolve antigenically, while others, like measles, do not (Fulton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Seasonal influenza vaccines must be reformulated on a nearly annual basis.
source: Because of this, seasonal influenza vaccines must be reformulated on a nearly annual basis, while measles vaccines typically provide lifelong protection.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about vaccine requirements.

claim: Measles vaccines typically provide lifelong protection.
source: Because of this, seasonal influenza vaccines must be reformulated on a nearly annual basis, while measles vaccines typically provide lifelong protection.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about vaccine effectiveness.

claim: In a 1980s human challenge study, subjects who were re-inoculated with the same 229E strain after about a year did not show symptoms or shed virus.
source: All subjects developed symptoms and shed virus upon initial virus inoculation. After about a year, subjects who were re-inoculated with the same strain did not show symptoms or shed virus.
evidence: This is a description of results from a cited study (Reed, 1984).

claim: In a 1980s human challenge study, the majority of subjects who were re-inoculated with a heterologous 229E strain developed symptoms and shed virus.
source: However, the majority of subjects who were re-inoculated with a heterologous strain developed symptoms and shed virus.
evidence: This is a description of results from a cited study (Reed, 1984).

claim: Immunity mounted against 229E viruses provides protection against some, but not all, other 229E strains.
source: This suggests that immunity mounted against 229E viruses provides protection against some, but not all, other 229E strains.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the human challenge study results.

claim: Eight OC43 genotypes have been identified.
source: More recent studies have identified eight OC43 genotypes and, in East Asian populations, certain genotypes were shown to temporally replace other genotypes (Lau et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In East Asian populations, certain OC43 genotypes temporally replace other genotypes.
source: More recent studies have identified eight OC43 genotypes and, in East Asian populations, certain genotypes were shown to temporally replace other genotypes (Lau et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Evidence for selection in the spike protein of a dominant OC43 genotype has been provided by dN/dS analysis.
source: However, evidence for selection in the spike protein of one of these dominant OC43 genotypes has been provided by dN/dS, a standard computational method for detecting positive selection (Ren et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: dN/dS analysis has been used to suggest positive selection in the spike protein of 229E.
source: This method has also been used to suggest positive selection in the spike protein of 229E (Chibo and Birch, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Two genetically distinct groupings of OC43 viruses alternate in prevalence within a Japanese community.
source: Additionally, two genetically distinct groupings (each of which include multiple of the aforementioned eight genotypes) of OC43 viruses have been shown to alternate in prevalence within a Japanese community, meaning that the majority of OC43 infections are caused by one group for about 2–4 years at which point the other group begins to account for the bulk of infections.
evidence: This is supported by inference from cited research.

claim: Antigenic differences between OC43 groups may contribute to epidemic switching.
source: It has been suggested that antigenic differences between these groups contribute to this epidemic switching (Komabayashi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from cited research.

claim: NL63 genotypes persist for relatively long periods of time in Kilifi, Kenya.
source: However, a similar surveillance of the NL63 genotypes circulating in Kilifi, Kenya found that NL63 genotypes persist for relatively long periods of time, that people become reinfected by the same genotype, and that reinfections are often enhanced by prior infection (Kiyuka et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: People become reinfected by the same NL63 genotype.
source: However, a similar surveillance of the NL63 genotypes circulating in Kilifi, Kenya found that NL63 genotypes persist for relatively long periods of time, that people become reinfected by the same genotype, and that reinfections are often enhanced by prior infection (Kiyuka et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: NL63 reinfections are often enhanced by prior infection.
source: However, a similar surveillance of the NL63 genotypes circulating in Kilifi, Kenya found that NL63 genotypes persist for relatively long periods of time, that people become reinfected by the same genotype, and that reinfections are often enhanced by prior infection (Kiyuka et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The findings about NL63 in Kenya are inconsistent with antigenic evolution in NL63.
source: These findings are inconsistent with antigenic evolution in NL63.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited findings about NL63.

claim: The study does not observe evidence for adaptive evolution in the spike protein of HKU1 and NL63.
source: Though we conduct these analyses on HKU1 and NL63, we do not observe evidence for adaptive evolution in the spike protein of these viruses.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's findings based on the data analysis.

claim: There is not enough longitudinal sequencing data available for HKU1 to confidently make conclusions about adaptive evolution.
source: For HKU1, there is not enough longitudinal sequencing data available for us to confidently make conclusions as to whether or not this lack of evidence reflects an actual lack of adaptive evolution.
evidence: This is a statement about data limitations affecting the conclusions.

claim: OC43 and 229E phylogenies form ladder-like topologies with isolate tips arranged into temporal clusters rather than geographic clusters.
source: Additionally, the trees form ladder-like topologies with isolate tips arranged into temporal clusters rather than geographic clusters, indicating a single global population rather than geographically isolated populations of virus.
evidence: This is an observation from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: OC43 and 229E represent single global populations rather than geographically isolated populations.
source: Additionally, the trees form ladder-like topologies with isolate tips arranged into temporal clusters rather than geographic clusters, indicating a single global population rather than geographically isolated populations of virus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the phylogenetic topology.

claim: The OC43 phylogeny bifurcates immediately from the root.
source: The phylogeny of OC43 bifurcates immediately from the root (Figure 1), indicating that OC43 consists of multiple, co-evolving lineages.
evidence: This is directly observable in Figure 1 and stated in the text.

claim: OC43 consists of multiple, co-evolving lineages.
source: The phylogeny of OC43 bifurcates immediately from the root (Figure 1), indicating that OC43 consists of multiple, co-evolving lineages.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the phylogenetic structure shown in Figure 1.

claim: The clock rate estimate is 5 × 10⁻⁴ substitutions per nucleotide site per year for OC43.
source: The clock rate estimate is 5 × 10–4 substitutions per nucleotide site per year for OC43 and 6 × 10–4 for 229E.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption and calculated from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The clock rate estimate is 6 × 10⁻⁴ substitutions per nucleotide site per year for 229E.
source: The clock rate estimate is 5 × 10–4 substitutions per nucleotide site per year for OC43 and 6 × 10–4 for 229E.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption and calculated from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Recombination is common among coronaviruses.
source: Because recombination is common among coronaviruses (Pasternak et al., 2006; Hon et al., 2008; Lau et al., 2011), we built separate phylogenies for each viral gene.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Comparing RdRp and spike trees reveals a pattern of recombination in some OC43 isolates.
source: Comparing the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) and spike trees reveals this pattern of recombination in some isolates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the tanglegram analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Comparison of S1 and S2 trees shows more limited evidence for intragenic recombination.
source: A comparison of the trees of the S1 and S2 sub-domains of spike shows more limited evidence for intragenic recombination (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), which is consistent with the fact that the distance between two genetic loci is inversely related to the chance that these loci remain linked during a recombination event.
evidence: This is an observation from the tanglegram analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The distance between two genetic loci is inversely related to the chance that these loci remain linked during a recombination event.
source: A comparison of the trees of the S1 and S2 sub-domains of spike shows more limited evidence for intragenic recombination (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), which is consistent with the fact that the distance between two genetic loci is inversely related to the chance that these loci remain linked during a recombination event.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about recombination.

claim: RdRp is expected to be under purifying selection due to its essential role in viral replication and lack of antibody exposure.
source: Because of its essential role in viral replication and lack of antibody exposure, we expect RdRp to be under purifying selection to maintain its structure and function.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on established knowledge about RdRp function.

claim: If HCoVs evolve antigenically, adaptive evolution is expected in the S1 domain of spike.
source: If HCoVs evolve antigenically, we expect to see adaptive evolution in spike, and particularly in the S1 domain of spike (Hofmann et al., 2006; Hulswit et al., 2019), due to its exposed location at the virion's surface and interaction with the host receptor.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The average number of substitutions per site is higher in S1 than S2 for OC43 and 229E.
source: The average number of substitutions per site is higher in S1 than S2 for HCoV lineages in OC43 and 229E (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Neutralizing antibodies bind to epitopes within the N-terminal domain as well as the RBD of S1.
source: We focus on S1 rather than the receptor-binding domain (RBD) within S1 in our analyses, because it is known that neutralizing antibodies bind to epitopes within the N-terminal domain (NTD) as well as the RBD of S1 (Liu et al., 2020a; Zhang et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The rate of nonsynonymous divergence is markedly higher within spike versus RdRp of 229E and OC43 lineage A.
source: The rate of nonsynonymous divergence is markedly higher within spike versus RdRp of 229E and OC43 lineage A (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Nonsynonymous divergence increases steadily over time in spike while remaining roughly constant at 0.0 in RdRp.
source: While nonsynonymous divergence increases steadily over time in spike, it remains roughly constant at 0.0 in RdRp.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is predominantly positive selection on OC43 and 229E spike.
source: These results suggest that there is predominantly positive selection on OC43 and 229E spike, but predominantly purifying selection on RdRp.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the divergence analysis results.

claim: There is predominantly purifying selection on RdRp.
source: These results suggest that there is predominantly positive selection on OC43 and 229E spike, but predominantly purifying selection on RdRp.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the divergence analysis results.

claim: The majority of nonsynonymous divergence in spike occurs within S1.
source: Separating spike into the S1 (receptor-binding) and S2 (membrane-fusion) domains reveals that the majority of nonsynonymous divergence in spike occurs within S1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The rates of nonsynonymous divergence in S2 are similar to those seen in RdRp.
source: In fact, the rates of nonsynonymous divergence in S2 are similar to those seen in RdRp, suggesting S2 evolves under purifying selection while S1 evolves adaptively.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: S2 evolves under purifying selection while S1 evolves adaptively.
source: In fact, the rates of nonsynonymous divergence in S2 are similar to those seen in RdRp, suggesting S2 evolves under purifying selection while S1 evolves adaptively.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the divergence analysis results.

claim: The ratio of nonsynonymous divergence in spike to nonsynonymous divergence in RdRp is consistently higher than the equivalent ratio of synonymous divergence.
source: However, the ratio of nonsynonymous divergence in spike to nonsynonymous divergence in RdRp is consistently higher than the equivalent ratio of synonymous divergence (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spike is accumulating relatively more nonsynonymous divergence than RdRp.
source: Thus, despite differences in synonymous divergence, spike is accumulating relatively more nonsynonymous divergence than RdRp.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the divergence ratio analysis.

claim: dN/dS estimates are higher in Spike than RdRp and higher in S1 than S2.
source: In agreement with measures of nonsynonymous divergence over time, dN/dS estimates are higher in Spike than RdRp and higher in S1 than S2 (Table 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Table 1.

claim: The estimate of dN/dS in OC43 spike is similar to the previously reported estimate of roughly 0.3.
source: Our estimate of dN/dS in OC43 spike is similar to the previously reported estimate of roughly 0.3 (Ren et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison of the study's results with previously published results.

claim: OC43 lineage A has continuously amassed adaptive substitutions in spike over the past >30 years.
source: As shown in Figure 4, OC43 lineage A has continuously amassed adaptive substitutions in spike over the past >30 years while RdRp has accrued few, if any, adaptive substitutions.
evidence: This is an observation from the Bhatt method analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: RdRp has accrued few, if any, adaptive substitutions over the past >30 years.
source: As shown in Figure 4, OC43 lineage A has continuously amassed adaptive substitutions in spike over the past >30 years while RdRp has accrued few, if any, adaptive substitutions.
evidence: This is an observation from the Bhatt method analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Adaptive substitutions in OC43 lineage A are located within the S1, and not the S2, domain of spike.
source: These adaptive substitutions are located within the S1, and not the S2, domain of spike (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the Bhatt method analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is a largely linear accumulation of adaptive substitutions in spike and S1 through time.
source: We observe a largely linear accumulation of adaptive substitutions in spike and S1 through time, although the method does not dictate a linear increase.
evidence: This is an observation from the Bhatt method analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Spike (and S1 in particular) is evolving in response to a continuous selective pressure.
source: This observation suggests that spike (and S1 in particular) is evolving in response to a continuous selective pressure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the linear accumulation of adaptive substitutions.

claim: OC43 lineage A accumulates roughly 1.8 × 10⁻³ adaptive substitutions per codon per year in the S1 domain of spike.
source: We estimate that OC43 lineage A accumulates roughly 1.8 × 10–3 adaptive substitutions per codon per year (or 1.4 adaptive amino acid substitutions in S1 each year) in the S1 domain of spike, while the rate of adaptation in OC43 lineage B is slightly higher and is estimated to result in an average 1.7 adaptive substitutions in S1 per year (Figure 5).
evidence: This is calculated from the Bhatt method analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: OC43 lineage A accumulates 1.4 adaptive amino acid substitutions in S1 each year.
source: We estimate that OC43 lineage A accumulates roughly 1.8 × 10–3 adaptive substitutions per codon per year (or 1.4 adaptive amino acid substitutions in S1 each year) in the S1 domain of spike, while the rate of adaptation in OC43 lineage B is slightly higher and is estimated to result in an average 1.7 adaptive substitutions in S1 per year (Figure 5).
evidence: This is calculated from the Bhatt method analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: OC43 lineage B accumulates an average 1.7 adaptive substitutions in S1 per year.
source: We estimate that OC43 lineage A accumulates roughly 1.8 × 10–3 adaptive substitutions per codon per year (or 1.4 adaptive amino acid substitutions in S1 each year) in the S1 domain of spike, while the rate of adaptation in OC43 lineage B is slightly higher and is estimated to result in an average 1.7 adaptive substitutions in S1 per year (Figure 5).
evidence: This is calculated from the Bhatt method analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The S1 domain of 229E accrues 0.76 adaptive substitutions per year.
source: The S1 domain of 229E is estimated to accrue 0.76 adaptive substitutions per year (a rate of 1.4 × 10–3 adaptive substitutions per codon per year).
evidence: This is calculated from the Bhatt method analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The receptor-binding domain of influenza A/H3N2 accumulates adaptive substitutions between two and three times faster than OC43 and 229E.
source: We estimate that the receptor-binding domain of influenza A/H3N2 accumulates adaptive substitutions between two and three times faster than the HCoVs OC43 and 229E (Figure 6).
evidence: This is calculated from the Bhatt method analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The rates of adaptive substitution in influenza B/Yam and B/Vic are on par with the seasonal HCoVs.
source: The rates of adaptive substitution in influenza B/Yam and B/Vic are on par with the seasonal HCoVs.
evidence: This is an observation from the Bhatt method analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: No adaptive substitutions are detected in the measles receptor-binding protein.
source: We detect no adaptive substitutions in the measles receptor-binding protein.
evidence: This is an observation from the Bhatt method analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The S1 domain of OC43 and 229E is under positive selection that generates new variants at about the same rate as influenza B strains.
source: These results put the evolution of the S1 domain of OC43 and 229E in context, indicating that the S1 domain is under positive selection, and that this positive selection generates new variants in the putative antigenic regions of these HCoVs at about the same rate as influenza B strains and about half the rate of the canonical example of antigenic evolution, the HA1 domain of influenza A/H3N2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The S1 domain of OC43 and 229E generates new variants at about half the rate of the HA1 domain of influenza A/H3N2.
source: These results put the evolution of the S1 domain of OC43 and 229E in context, indicating that the S1 domain is under positive selection, and that this positive selection generates new variants in the putative antigenic regions of these HCoVs at about the same rate as influenza B strains and about half the rate of the canonical example of antigenic evolution, the HA1 domain of influenza A/H3N2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparative analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Estimates of adaptive evolution are not biased by recombination events.
source: As the strength of positive selection increases, we detect a higher rate of adaptive evolution, regardless of the level of recombination (Figure 7). This demonstrates that our estimates of adaptive evolution are not biased by recombination events.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The average TMRCA is lower in spike than RdRp for both OC43 lineage A and 229E.
source: We observe that for both OC43 lineage A and 229E, the average TMRCA is lower in spike than RdRp and lower in S1 versus S2.
evidence: This is an observation from the TMRCA analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The average TMRCA is lower in S1 versus S2 for both OC43 lineage A and 229E.
source: We observe that for both OC43 lineage A and 229E, the average TMRCA is lower in spike than RdRp and lower in S1 versus S2.
evidence: This is an observation from the TMRCA analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The TMRCA results suggest strong directional selection in S1, likely driven by pressures to evade the humoral immune system.
source: These results suggest strong directional selection in S1, likely driven by pressures to evade the humoral immune system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the TMRCA analysis results.

claim: The difference in TMRCA between S1 and S2 is indicative of intra-spike recombination.
source: The difference in TMRCA between S1 and S2 is indicative not only of differing selective pressures acting on these two spike domains, but also of intra-spike recombination.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the TMRCA analysis results.

claim: HKU1 was identified in the early 2000s.
source: Because HKU1 was identified in the early 2000s, there are fewer longitudinally sequenced isolates available for this HCoV compared to 229E and OC43 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as background information about HKU1 discovery.

claim: There are fewer longitudinally sequenced isolates available for HKU1 compared to 229E and OC43.
source: Because HKU1 was identified in the early 2000s, there are fewer longitudinally sequenced isolates available for this HCoV compared to 229E and OC43 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation about data availability shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: When HKU1 is considered to consist of just one lineage, there is no signal of antigenic evolution by divergence analysis or by the Bhatt method.
source: When HKU1 is considered to consist of just one lineage, there is no signal of antigenic evolution by divergence analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or by the Bhatt method of estimating adaptive evolution (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the analyses shown in the referenced figures.

claim: When HKU1 is assumed to consist of two co-circulating lineages, HKU1 lineage A has a markedly higher rate of adaptive substitutions in S1 than in S2 or RdRp.
source: However, when HKU1 is assumed to consist of two co-circulating lineages, HKU1 lineage A has a markedly higher rate of adaptive substitutions in S1 than in S2 or RdRp (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the Bhatt method analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Less longitudinal data reduces the ability to detect adaptive evolution by skewing the estimated rate away from the 'truth' and increasing the uncertainty of the analysis.
source: This simulated data reveals a general trend that less longitudinal data reduces the ability to detect adaptive evolution by skewing the estimated rate away from the 'truth' and increasing the uncertainty of the analysis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: It is not appropriate to make strong conclusions about adaptive evolution, or lack thereof, in HKU1 given the dearth of longitudinal data.
source: Given the dearth of longitudinal data for HKU1, we do not feel that it is appropriate to make strong conclusions about adaptive evolution, or lack thereof, in this HCoV.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the analysis due to data availability.

claim: Substantially more NL63 isolates have been sequenced compared to HKU1.
source: Despite being identified at roughly the same time as HKU1, substantially more NL63 isolates have been sequenced (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) making the phylogenetic reconstruction and evolutionary analyses of this virus correspondingly more reliable.
evidence: This is an observation about data availability shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: No evidence for adaptive evolution is observed in NL63.
source: We do not observe evidence for adaptive evolution in NL63 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and this lack of support for adaptive evolution in the NL63 spike gene is more likely to reflect an actual lack of adaptive evolution in this virus.
evidence: This is an observation from the analyses shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The lack of support for adaptive evolution in NL63 is more likely to reflect an actual lack of adaptive evolution in this virus.
source: We do not observe evidence for adaptive evolution in NL63 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and this lack of support for adaptive evolution in the NL63 spike gene is more likely to reflect an actual lack of adaptive evolution in this virus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis results and data quality considerations.

claim: S1 accumulates between 0.8 (229E) and 1.4 (OC43) adaptive substitutions per year.
source: We observe that S1 accumulates between 0.8 (229E) and 1.4 (OC43) adaptive substitutions per year.
evidence: This is a summary of the Bhatt method analysis results.

claim: OC43 and 229E accumulate adaptive substitutions at roughly half the rate of influenza A/H3N2.
